tEn: Virtual Cells to Lab Compass: AI That Predicts and Steers Organoid Experiments
tZh: 从虚拟细胞到实验室指南针：预测并引导类器官实验的 AI
sEn: Fabian Theis discusses how virtual cell models evolved from mapping to prediction and now to steering experiments, including Lab Compass, an inverse generative model for reaching desired cellular states.
sZh: Fabian Theis 讲述虚拟细胞模型如何从图谱构建走向预测，并进一步引导实验，包括用于抵达目标细胞状态的逆向生成模型 Lab Compass。

consensus.en: Virtual cell models are shifting from mapping and prediction to actively steering the next experiment.
consensus.zh: 虚拟细胞模型正从映射和预测转向主动指导下一个实验。

consensus.en: Perturbation prediction is the core of virtual cells, but it requires world-model-like approaches beyond representation learning.
consensus.zh: 扰动预测是虚拟细胞的核心，但需要超越表示学习的世界模型式方法。

consensus.en: Data generation at scale, especially perturbation screens and organoids, is unlocking progress in virtual cell modeling.
consensus.zh: 大规模数据生成，尤其是扰动筛选和类器官，正在释放虚拟细胞建模的进展。

consensus.en: Scaling laws must be demonstrated for foundation models in biology to earn trust and adoption.
consensus.zh: 生物基础模型必须展示缩放定律才能赢得信任和采用。

consensus.en: The Y-model of co-advising between wet lab and computational PIs produces well-rounded scientists and impactful work.
consensus.zh: 湿实验与计算PI共同指导的Y模型培养出全面发展的科学家和具有影响力的工作。

consensus.en: Commercial success in virtual cell adjacent ideas often requires coupling with unique data generation or drug development.
consensus.zh: 虚拟细胞相关想法的商业成功通常需要与独特的数据生成或药物开发相结合。

contrarian.en: Linear baselines often outperform complex deep learning models in perturbation prediction, especially for subtle effects.
contrarian.zh: 在扰动预测中，线性基线往往优于复杂的深度学习模型，尤其是对于细微效应。

contrarian.en: Strong inductive biases can hurt predictive power; flexible data-driven models with post-hoc interpretation are better.
contrarian.zh: 强归纳偏置可能损害预测能力；灵活的数据驱动模型加上事后解释更好。

contrarian.en: The virtual cell challenge revealed that metric design, not just model architecture, is a key bottleneck.
contrarian.zh: 虚拟细胞挑战赛揭示，指标设计而不仅仅是模型架构是关键瓶颈。

contrarian.en: Europe's startup ecosystem excels at creation but lags in scaling due to lack of large VC risk capital.
contrarian.zh: 欧洲的创业生态系统在创建方面出色，但由于缺乏大型风险资本而在规模化方面落后。

contrarian.en: Platform-only AI biology companies often pivot to drug development because pure platform monetization is unclear.
contrarian.zh: 纯平台型AI生物公司往往转向药物开发，因为纯平台变现不明确。

contrarian.en: Fully autonomous labs with robotics are premature; active learning with human-in-the-loop is more realistic now.
contrarian.zh: 带机器人的全自动实验室为时过早；当前更现实的是有人类在环的主动学习。

turns.en: Welcome to the Latent Space AI for Science podcast. I'm RJ Honicky, CTO of Miro Omics. I'm joined by my co-host Brandon Anderson, who develops RNA therapeutics at Atomic AI. I can't emphasize enough how much Fabian Theis and his labs and companies have contributed to the development of systems biology and various iterations of the virtual cell concept. Papers and models come out of his lab faster than I can read them, and the lab is consistently moving the ball forward on our understanding of how to observe and model the behaviors and the interactions of cells. Just as importantly, his work often focuses on creating the tools that researchers and scientists actually use in their day-to-day work. Most computational biologists have probably used Scanpy and AnnData at some point. And this work has led to the creation of SCverse, which is an amazing collection of open tools that's attracted many many contributors. Of course, Fabian is one of those academics who has way more honors than you can possibly list, but suffice it to say that he leads a bunch of the AI and computational biology efforts at Helmholtz Munich and related institutions, and participates also in many other industry efforts. Fabian, it's really great to meet you. Thanks a lot for joining us.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到 Latent Space AI for Science 播客。我是 RJ Honicky，Miro Omics 的首席技术官。和我一起的是联合主持人 Brandon Anderson，他在 Atomic AI 开发 RNA 疗法。我怎么强调 Fabian Theis 和他的实验室及公司对系统生物学发展以及虚拟细胞概念各种迭代的贡献都不为过。他实验室发表的论文和模型比我读得还快，而且实验室一直在推动我们对如何观察和建模细胞行为与相互作用的理解。同样重要的是，他的工作常常专注于创建研究人员和科学家日常实际使用的工具。大多数计算生物学家可能都用过 Scanpy 和 AnnData。这项工作促成了 SCverse 的创建，这是一个了不起的开放工具集合，吸引了许多许多贡献者。当然，Fabian 是那种荣誉多到列不完的学者之一，但 suffice it to say，他在 Helmholtz Munich 及相关机构领导着一批 AI 和计算生物学工作，也参与许多其他行业项目。Fabian，很高兴见到你。非常感谢你加入我们。

turns.en: Thanks for having me. I'm really looking forward to the discussion, man.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请。我非常期待这次讨论，伙计。

turns.en: Yeah, I've been tracking your work for a long time, and so it's a great honor to finally get you on the show and talk to you.
turns.zh: 是的，我关注你的工作很久了，所以很荣幸终于能请你上节目和你聊聊。

turns.en: Let's kick things off with some of the hype happening right now. There's a ton of interest right now in structural biology, Anthropic and OpenAI biopharma initiatives focus heavily on designing molecules right now. On the other hand, virtual cell and systems biology approaches really haven't gotten as much attention recently. Maybe Zera and Noetik are good counterexamples there, but Biohub just announced a $1.8 billion collaboration with the DOE, NIH, Meta, and Google to collect and open-source multiscale biological data that can be used to develop a new generation of virtual cells. So, my question, do you think that we're about to see renewed interest from the pharma industry in virtual cells based on the activity that we're seeing in academia right now?
turns.zh: 让我们从当前的一些热点话题开始。现在结构生物学有大量关注，Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的生物制药计划目前重点放在设计分子上。另一方面，虚拟细胞和系统生物学方法最近确实没有获得那么多关注。也许 Zera 和 Noetik 是很好的反例，但 Biohub 刚刚宣布与 DOE、NIH、Meta 和 Google 合作，投入 18 亿美元收集并开源多尺度生物数据，用于开发新一代虚拟细胞。所以我的问题是，基于我们目前在学术界看到的活动，你认为制药行业即将对虚拟细胞重新产生兴趣吗？

turns.en: I should disclose before I sort of go to the answer that obviously my opinion is quite academic in the sense that whenever I talk to my friends and colleagues that really sort of day-by-day sit in the startups, they have like what I sort of have as an overview and sort of a bit of intuition what the different research labs do, they have the same thing for the startups. And they know this is sort of the hot big thing that, you know, this and this investments are happening. I don't really have that on that scale. But having said that, for example, you may you mentioned a Biohub's initiative, which by the way is also heavily coupled to human cell atlas, which is sort of this international really worldwide consortium that sort of pushes this next level of data set generation. I do think that there's a whole bunch of reasons why we going to see that sort of scale up from all these models working well in terms of being generative, but also sort of lap in the loop on the molecule level now being exported and sort of really working one level up on the cell level. And I think there's a bunch of reasons for that. And the first one I think it maybe the most important one, which you really hit here, is the data generation. I think we had that concept of a virtual cell for a while, but my lab we started this perturbation prediction modeling and using machine learning in 2019 with a paper we called SEGAN at the time, which was like it was a non-linear model, but essentially sort of in the latent space did some linear transformation. And it was actually quite okay, and even nowadays many of these sort of pseudo-linear type of things are still doing a good job, but the reason for that being that I think the data sets and the questions that we asked on top were just sort of still on the simplistic side. That's why also sort of it didn't yet take up. So whenever people talk about virtual cells, maybe also your question, I think what you actually ask is how does Can you predict how a cell would behave under all kind of perturbations? And that's sort of I think a quite deep question. If you really think about it, it's maybe even a bit of a holy grail in computational biology systems biology. Sort of this input-output system that is a cell with memory and like with all these specifications and with all the different sort of levels of molecules and so on, not just RNA. I think being able to map this out, what does even understanding mean? And I've been this sort of a bit of a meta problem, but I think you understand or at least you model a system very well when you sort of predict its output behavior given different inputs. So I think it's a very good question, and this is why often people nowadays equate a virtual cell with perturbation prediction. I think it's a bit too simplistic, but I think these perturbation prediction type of models and that's sort of being a maybe what you mean by virtual cell is taking off a lot in the startup landscape. I think it's a bit exploding there because I think a lot about US Europe, but also in the Chinese ecosystem there's a lot of these additional efforts now happening. And I hope that these are not just sort of now a kindling of a flame because everyone sort of adds AI to their things, but because pharma is really desperately needing to be cell type context-specific in their screens, which at the moment they can't do yet.
turns.zh: 在回答之前我应该说明，显然我的观点相当学术，因为每当我与那些真正每天在初创公司里的朋友和同事交谈时，他们对我所拥有的那种概览和对不同研究实验室所做工作的一点直觉，他们对初创公司也有同样的了解。他们知道这是热门大事，知道这些投资正在发生。我并没有那种规模的了解。但话虽如此，例如你提到了 Biohub 的倡议，顺便说一句，这也与人类细胞图谱紧密耦合，那是一个国际性的真正全球联盟，推动下一代数据集生成。我确实认为有很多原因让我们会看到这种规模扩大，所有这些模型在生成方面表现良好，而且现在在分子层面被导出并真正在细胞层面更上一层楼地工作。我认为有很多原因。第一个我认为可能是最重要的，就是你真正指出的数据生成。我认为我们拥有虚拟细胞的概念已有一段时间，但我的实验室在 2019 年就开始做扰动预测建模并使用机器学习，当时我们称之为 SEGAN 的论文，那是一个非线性模型，但本质上在潜在空间做了一些线性变换。它实际上相当不错，即使现在许多这类伪线性类型的东西仍然表现良好，但原因是我认为数据集和我们在此基础上提出的问题仍然偏简单。这就是为什么它还没有真正兴起。所以每当人们谈论虚拟细胞，也许你的问题，我认为你实际问的是：你能预测细胞在所有扰动下会如何行为吗？我认为这是一个相当深刻的问题。如果你真的想一想，这甚至可能是计算生物学系统生物学的一个圣杯。这个输入输出系统，一个细胞，有记忆，有所有这些规格，有所有不同层次的分子等等，不仅仅是 RNA。我认为能够绘制出这些，甚至理解意味着什么？我一直觉得这有点像一个元问题，但我认为当你能够预测系统在不同输入下的输出行为时，你至少很好地建模了它。所以我认为这是一个很好的问题，这就是为什么现在人们常常将虚拟细胞等同于扰动预测。我认为这有点过于简单化，但我认为这些扰动预测类型的模型——也许这就是你所说的虚拟细胞——在初创领域正在大量兴起。我认为那里有点爆发，因为我多考虑美国和欧洲，但在中国生态系统中现在也有许多这些额外的努力。我希望这些不仅仅是每个人都在给自己的东西加 AI 而点燃的火花，而是因为制药公司真的迫切需要在筛选中做到细胞类型上下文特异性，而目前他们还做不到。

turns.en: I mean for me, if I may, you stop me when I'm getting too much into these old stories. I've been a trained machine learning scientist for the longest time doing all kinds of things, but I started with single cell early on qPCR. Maybe initially, if I'm really honest, not so much because it was the biology that I was interested in, but because we had high sample numbers, purely for that, right? Because even earlier on it was clear that the number of qPCRs at scale, but then of course transcriptomes was just getting really big. And when I started my career earlier on, we had like a few bug RNA, now we sort of had thousands of them or whatever, right? So this is like early times. But now we're going to a regime, and that was one of these eye-opening moments when PacBio had like I think they called it the giga lab or something like that. And there's similar ones from competing companies now, but when they had like in a single experiment 10 million transcriptomes measured, right? I felt that was like next-level stuff, and this step from just getting more PBMCs as a control tool, like let's actually do something at scale to it sort of having here the cell space, but then having here the perturbation space, which typically was very scarce. It was like control versus disease or so. So this sort of number of points what you had here in terms of sampling on the perturbation space was typically much more scarce than the number of observations in terms of cells that you had. But now this is exploding. Now you sort of have, I don't know, 100 different cell lines where you do sort of full perturb-seq like full CRISPR, or you have like batteries of 1,000 drugs or so added, and suddenly this space gets really rich, right? And then you can start doing all these fancy perturbation prediction type of things. And this is currently happening. It's crazy what scale it's happening. We are ourselves involved in a whole bunch of things where we actually go beyond cell lines and do organoid perturbations, and maybe if you have time we can talk a bit more about that because I'm quite convinced that we need to go to multi-cellular systems to have actually really interesting readouts, but I think everyone is scaling these levels up, and at some point, we're going to go maybe even to human genetics as a perturbation.
turns.zh: 对我来说，如果可以的话，当我太深入这些老故事时你就打断我。我长期以来一直是一名受过训练的机器学习科学家，做各种各样的事情，但我早期是从单细胞 qPCR 开始的。也许最初，说实话，并不是因为我对生物学感兴趣，而是因为我们有高样本数，纯粹是为了这个，对吧？因为更早的时候就已经清楚，规模化的 qPCR 数量，然后当然转录组，变得非常庞大。当我早期开始职业生涯时，我们只有几个 bug RNA，现在我们有数千个之类的，对吧？所以这是早期。但现在我们进入了一个新阶段，那是令人大开眼界的时刻之一，当 PacBio 有——我想他们称之为 giga lab 之类的。现在竞争公司也有类似的，但当他们在一次实验中测量了 1000 万个转录组时，对吧？我觉得那是下一个层次的东西，从仅仅获取更多 PBMC 作为对照工具，到实际上在规模上做些什么，这里有了细胞空间，但还有扰动空间，后者通常非常稀缺。就像对照 versus 疾病之类的。所以这里在扰动空间采样方面的点数通常比你在细胞方面的观察数量要稀缺得多。但现在这在爆炸式增长。现在你有，我不知道，100 种不同的细胞系，你做全 perturb-seq 像全 CRISPR，或者你有 1000 种药物之类的组合添加，突然这个空间变得非常丰富，对吧？然后你可以开始做所有这些花哨的扰动预测类型的事情。这目前正在发生。发生的规模令人疯狂。我们自己参与了一大堆事情，我们实际上超越了细胞系，做类器官扰动，也许如果你有时间我们可以多谈谈这个，因为我相当确信我们需要进入多细胞系统才能有真正有趣的读数，但我认为每个人都在扩大这些水平，在某个时候，我们甚至可能将人类遗传学作为扰动。

turns.en: When I give public talks I typically say, you know, human genome project, we sort of have the genome for the body, but it's pretty much the same everywhere, right? So why do we have all these different cell types, right? What's happening specifically? And one of the first levels is that per cell different stuff is being read off of the genome, right? And these messenger RNAs, which then encode the various downstream proteins, well, these are differently expressed, as one says, in different cells. And in a human maybe there's something like 20,000 different types of these, and with splicing many many more, but that's the rough level. So what you de facto have is per cell a 20,000 dimensional vector that has a whole bunch of zeros and stuff is not there, but then a whole bunch of numbers, how many of these counts of these messenger RNAs you have. Because these things are called transcripts, right? This is called then the transcriptome. Yeah, and de facto then you have this 20,000 dimensional space that you very often encode in a nicer latent space that has like a sub-manifold, like this subspace where this actual cell cloud lives, right? And if the cell cloud then like these 20,000 dimensional vectors, each point then being one cell, right? If they cluster up, then we call these things cell types or something like that. And if they go into a sausage or whatever, right? We call them into trajectories, like a cell differentiation, like the fertilized egg cell then making all the cell types in the body or something like that.

turns.en: Maybe even something as basic as when you go to these in vitro systems where pharma does drug screens, when you put them in a dish, you can do different what's called media conditions and they also have so much impact, right? And it's still a bit bio-driven for me, maybe even like alchemy, what type of cocktails people come up with to then take skin cells and turn them into more or less embryo-like state cells, right? Where you can then make new cells to heal different stuff in the body, or these what they call the Yamanaka factors, for example. These were Nobel laureate type of stuff, right? So I think having a space of perturbations, essentially of things that you can do to a cell, this can be a very rich thing. It can go as far as changes in the gene, which would be like a full knockout, or something more subtle, which is sort of human genetics. And I think all of that we need to put in a big space of stuff that we can do that has an influence on cell state. And a virtual cell model should take all of it, right? And also combinations thereof, of course. And maybe disease happening, time, whatever, that then impacts that.
turns.zh: 也许甚至像这样基础的事情：当你使用这些体外系统时，制药公司做药物筛选，当你把它们放在培养皿中，你可以做不同的所谓培养基条件，它们也有很大的影响，对吧？对我来说，这仍然有点生物驱动，甚至像炼金术，人们想出什么样的混合物，然后取皮肤细胞，把它们变成或多或少像胚胎状态的细胞，对吧？然后你可以制造新细胞来治愈身体的不同部位，或者他们所说的山中因子。这些是诺贝尔奖级别的成果，对吧？所以我认为有一个扰动空间，本质上是对细胞可以做的事情，这可能是一个非常丰富的东西。它可以深入到基因的改变，比如完全敲除，或者更微妙的东西，比如人类遗传学。我认为所有这些我们都需要放入一个大的空间，我们可以做的对细胞状态有影响的事情。而一个虚拟细胞模型应该接受所有这些，对吧？当然还有它们的组合。也许还有疾病发生、时间等等，然后影响那个。

turns.en: That's a great connection to the organoids idea. So can you talk a little bit about—okay, so an organoid is what? And how does that connect to this concept of perturbation space? And what do you do to it in addition to it just this context?
turns.zh: 这与类器官的想法有很好的联系。所以你能谈谈——好吧，那么类器官是什么？它如何与扰动空间这个概念联系起来？除了这个背景之外，你还对它做了什么？

turns.en: Dude, when I first heard about—learned about this concept, I should say, you know, I'm an overtrained biologist, so I typically learn about things when I read a bit or when I talk to colleagues and friends. And when I first saw that people are able to take a cell—actually cells out of a body of a cancer cell or whatever, right?—and let them then grow into small multicellular systems that actually cells start connecting to things, I was super super impressed. So, you know, people can now, for example, take some cells, put them in a dish, and then grow little mini brains, essentially a set of neurons that essentially really start connecting, talking to each other. And people have shown that they can get those sort of mini brains in a dish to compute. Similarly, people can take heart cells, grow them into little heart organoids. We have a bunch of local collaborations with fantastic partners that actually start beating. Like you have beating little heart cell clumps in a dish, right? And then of course, once you have these—and it's the same thing as I spoke about brain—there's even simpler systems like the colon where this works very well. There's a whole bunch of cancer systems. But also for, let's say, if you want to study diseases with hard to acquire material. Let's say you want to look into the genetics of some type of neurodegenerative diseases or so. Typically it's very hard to get access to tissue, right? So you take stem cells from the skin—you take cells from the skin, differentiate and turn them into these mini little brains, and then you can potentially study some things there. So I think this concept of replicating little bits of organs, it's what they call organoids, in a dish is very fascinating. There's all kinds of limitations, obviously. Often immune cells—the immune system is missing. There's like no—maybe feeding them or something like that. So there's all kinds of problems, right? But it's much much more than just a cell line which is like one cell type.
turns.zh: 老兄，当我第一次听说——了解到这个概念时，我应该说，你知道，我是一个过度训练的生物学家，所以我通常通过阅读一点或与同事和朋友交谈来了解事物。当我第一次看到人们能够取一个细胞——实际上是从身体中取出细胞，比如癌细胞之类的，对吧？——然后让它们生长成小的多细胞系统，细胞实际上开始相互连接，我超级超级印象深刻。所以，你知道，人们现在可以，例如，取一些细胞，放在培养皿中，然后生长出小迷你大脑，本质上是一组神经元，它们真正开始连接、相互交流。人们已经证明他们可以让培养皿中的那些迷你大脑进行计算。同样，人们可以取心脏细胞，将它们生长成小心脏类器官。我们与出色的合作伙伴有一些本地合作，它们实际上开始跳动。就像你在培养皿中有跳动的小心脏细胞团，对吧？然后当然，一旦你有了这些——这和我说的脑一样——还有更简单的系统，比如结肠，这非常有效。有一大堆癌症系统。但也可以说，如果你想研究难以获取材料的疾病。比如你想研究某种神经退行性疾病的遗传学。通常很难获得组织，对吧？所以你从皮肤取干细胞——你从皮肤取细胞，分化并变成这些迷你小大脑，然后你可以在那里潜在地研究一些东西。所以我认为这种复制器官小部分的概念，就是他们所说的类器官，在培养皿中非常迷人。显然有各种各样的限制。通常免疫细胞——免疫系统缺失。可能没有——也许喂养它们之类的。所以有各种各样的问题，对吧？但它远比只是一个细胞系——那是一种细胞类型——要丰富得多。

turns.en: Moving to the modeling side, how do you model that?

turns.en: So that's I think at the research frontier. So I don't think people have agreed on what the optimum way to model is, particularly also because there's not as much data as one wants. Jay, right? You're involved, if I understand correctly, in a whole bunch of spatial omics slash also H&E sort of pathology type of effort. So like pathology, there's so much samples available, right? And now increasingly we sort of do a bit more spatial omics. So I think how we even represent spatially connected data sets. And then you also have to break it down on an organoid level and so on. But this is just us putting categories on top of stuff. But it helps us understand this complexity. I don't think we have a similar metaphor for local niches of cells. Maybe a little bit, but also in H&E, right? Whenever I talk and see what pathologists do, it's often very qualitative and it's maybe not at that level yet. So I think we need to develop a bit of a categorization language for us. turns.zh: 所以我认为这处于研究前沿。所以我不认为人们已经就最佳建模方式达成一致，特别是也因为数据没有人们想要的那么多。Jay，对吧？如果我理解正确，你参与了一大堆空间组学以及 H&E 病理类型的工作。所以像病理学，有那么多样本可用，对吧？现在越来越多地我们做一点空间组学。所以我认为我们甚至如何表示空间连接的数据集。然后你还必须在类器官层面分解等等。人们不像对解离细胞那样清楚。所以再次，把它简单一点，我认为如果我们看解离细胞的空间，看这些群体，我们有这个美丽的比喻，我们人类称之为细胞类型，而自然并不关心。但这只是我们在东西上面放类别。但它帮助我们理解这种复杂性。我不认为我们对细胞的局部微环境有类似的比喻。也许有一点，但在 H&E 中也是如此，对吧？每当我交谈并看到病理学家做什么时，它通常非常定性，也许还没有达到那个水平。所以我认为我们需要为我们开发一点分类语言。也许计算上，也许我们不需要这么多，但计算上我们也需要思考一下如何处理这个。目前我们基本上将其视为细胞的分布。所以这是目前的解决方案，但我认为它可以更加微妙，比如图之类的。

turns.en: So, on the one hand you have the bitter lesson and you know, sort of you remove inductive bias and you end up being able to have a larger data set that's applicable to your problem and then that helps you to get more accurate models because the distribution is wider and whatever. So that's like the one and then but then there's this like countervailing tendency which is like maybe you could call it the anti-bitter lesson or like the other the flip side of the bitter lesson where when you're in data poor regimes for one thing then you have to introduce a lot of inductive bias to get enough statistical power to make good inferences. But there's also a second side of that which I think John Platt in our discussion with him not too long ago brought up was that you have these like predictive and then descriptive models. And what you really want as a scientist is to get to a simplification a descriptive model where you can say, "Oh well, I've tested all the apples and the gravity works in such a way on apples." And then but I'm modeling this as a universal concept with simply so that we know that it works on plants as well. Right? And so that I want to understand from you, what are the simplifications or you know, sort of maybe simplifications, maybe insights, maybe actual mathematical or otherwise scientific models that are becoming apparent that are going to help to reduce all the complexity so that we're able to actually make meaningful gain meaningful understanding from these really large data sets.
turns.zh: 所以，一方面你有苦涩的教训，你知道，你移除归纳偏置，你最终能够拥有一个适用于你问题的更大的数据集，然后这帮助你获得更准确的模型，因为分布更广等等。所以那是其中之一，但然后有这种抵消的趋势，也许你可以称之为反苦涩的教训，或者像苦涩教训的另一面，当你在数据贫乏的情况下，对于一件事，你必须引入大量的归纳偏置来获得足够的统计功效以做出好的推断。但还有第二个方面，我认为 John Platt 在我们不久前与他的讨论中提出，你有这些预测模型和描述模型。而作为科学家，你真正想要的是达到简化，一个描述模型，你可以说：“哦，我测试了所有的苹果，重力对苹果的作用是这样的。”然后但我将其建模为一个普遍概念，简单地以便我们知道它也适用于植物。对吧？所以我想从你那里了解，有哪些简化——或者你知道，也许是简化，也许是见解，也许是实际的数学或其他科学模型——正在变得明显，将有助于减少所有的复杂性，以便我们能够从这些真正大的数据集中实际获得有意义的收获、有意义的理解。

turns.en: Yeah, that's a very important, I think kind of deep point, which I think sort of breaks the field into maybe two different groups of people with answers, right? So how much do we need to put inductive biases, maybe priors into a model to maybe make it better explainable, right? But potentially also more robust in going out of distribution. Or how much are we going to just rely on bigger data to sort of have the model be more expressive and so on. And I think there I need to be very clear before we may go into the full philosophy. I think literature has really clearly shown over, I think now decades, at least for all of us, very many data sets that if we build an a priori inductive biases too strongly, that we might lose predictive power, right? So it comes at a cost. So, and if you know, let's say you're a physician and you just want to, or maybe even if you're a patient and you maybe you might have cancer or not, maybe you want to have the best model as a predictor. Maybe she getting treated, you want to have a model that is maybe a bit less good, but you understand it a bit more. But for the prediction, at least I think you want to have the best. And this is I think not entirely clear. And I think in our field with this perturbation space scale, the cell scale I think is big, but the perturbation space scale, like the stuff that we do to it not being as big, I don't think we're yet in the super data rich regime. So, I think in our case these hybrid models might be still the thing to go for, but more and more of course, and this is I think this I don't know if you can call it sad, but the honest learning from big scale machine learning is that at some point data beats human-made additional concepts in these models. And I know at least one simple example I often put is AlphaFold, where you know, the first model sort of made this extraordinary effort to make the molecules rotation invariant, they sort of built it into the learning process, and only in later versions, you know, sort of rotation symmetry was automatically found by the model just with more data and was a bit more flexible because whatever physical constraint you put in, it's not always as rigid, and then you sort of you gain something if you let the model learn from this. So, I think in the future the bigger part at least of the sort of more used models will be those more flexible, very much database ones, where you then a posteriori put the interpretation on top.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个非常重要、我觉得有点深刻的观点，它把领域分成了两类人，对吧？我们需要在模型里加入多少归纳偏置、先验，来让它更可解释，同时可能对分布外数据更鲁棒？还是我们只依赖更多数据，让模型更有表现力等等。在深入哲学之前，我需要说清楚：文献已经非常清楚地表明，几十年来，至少对我们所有人、很多数据集来说，如果我们把先验归纳偏置建得太强，可能会损失预测能力，对吧？所以是有代价的。如果你是一名医生，或者甚至你是一名患者，可能得了癌症也可能没有，也许你想要最好的预测模型。也许在接受治疗时，你想要一个稍微差一点但你能理解的模型。但至少对于预测，我想你会想要最好的。这一点我觉得并不完全清楚。在我们领域，扰动空间的规模，细胞规模我觉得很大，但扰动空间的规模，比如我们对它做的事情没那么大，我不认为我们已经处于超级数据丰富的状态。所以，在我们这种情况下，这些混合模型可能仍然是首选，但当然会越来越多，这是我从大规模机器学习中学到的诚实教训，不知道能不能叫悲伤，但就是：在某个时刻，数据会战胜人类额外添加的概念。我经常举的一个简单例子是 AlphaFold，第一个模型做出了非凡的努力，让分子具有旋转不变性，把它建到学习过程中，而只有在后来的版本中，旋转对称性才被模型自动发现，只需更多数据，而且更灵活，因为无论你加入什么物理约束，它并不总是那么刚性，如果你让模型从中学习，你会有所收获。所以，我认为未来，至少更多被使用的模型将是那些更灵活的、非常依赖数据的模型，然后你再事后把解释加在上面。

turns.en: This also brings up the question for me. So, you actually I think recently wrote or co-authored a paper on the statistical power that the current generation of virtual cells have in terms of the data, the lift that you get from additional data in those current generation of virtual cell models. And I think you had said basically that the objective function or the training methodology is potentially the problem there and not necessarily that the information is not in the data. So, like what can you explain that a little bit and why you think that maybe there's plenty of untapped information in the information and then like what where does that get us and what do we need to do to get further?
turns.zh: 这也让我想到一个问题。你最近写了一篇或合著了一篇论文，关于当前一代虚拟细胞在数据方面的统计功效，即从额外数据中获得的提升。我想你基本上说过，目标函数或训练方法可能是问题所在，而不一定是信息不在数据中。所以，你能解释一下吗？为什么你认为信息中可能有大量未开发的信息？然后这能带我们到哪里？我们需要做什么才能更进一步？

turns.en: Yeah, I think it's fair to say that early on we had some very small, more limited prediction models of learning, let's say latent spaces first and then also perturbations on top. And then, you know, when these really large-scale foundation model representations came out everyone was sort of buying into the hype and maybe potentially sort of bit over buying then, you know, obviously after this you know, comes what's it called the sobering up value or something like that. And then there were a whole bunch of papers coming up where they were basically saying, you know, hey, maybe even more or less linear model were doing good job. And actually now I see gen paper early on we had already some of these benchmarks showing that it's not so super easy and simple task is just to improve on that. I think there's a truth to it that the particular in the current data state for some things let's say you want to predict the effect of a crisper in a cell and you might not need the most fancy model. Whereas if you ask a bit or if you want to predict a cell type or something like that, you know, for that mostly logistic regression is fine. But if you want to predict something a bit more difficult, for example, in our niche former paper which is a foundation model for spatial omics, we showed we had a new task which we introduced where you say you have a you have the gene expression you have sort of the state in latent space of a single cell, can you predict the gene expression state of its neighboring cells? Because you know, they're always in communication or maybe the other way around. So, like they're always in communication, so because you know, they talk to each other you sort of see a remnant of that sort of cell state in this one. And then actually this is harder to do and if you sort of have these harder tasks you need the stronger more linear things and you particularly need to look for more subtle data. So, your question, can you sort of find out more sort of information which type of things I think very much depends on what you sort of ask at the end of it. Of course, like in the self-supervised learning phase, I think we're definitely not there yet with the best way how we represent how we learn these things. There's a lot of copying of what happens in NLP type of LLMs, right? And like masked autoencoders are always the typical way to go, but the type of losses, the type of representations, I think people are still debating. Maybe because you know, this is sort of often kind of tabular data, so you can just like tabular foundation models and all sorts of being tried out. There's a lot of JEPA type of approaches now because it's like we have one thing where we use contrastive learning. So it's just people playing around with the losses, but also with the representations. And I think nowadays reviewers, and at least I've been advocating this for a long time, are really much more closer looking that you really properly show scaling laws. This was what has missed from the early papers of the foundation models, and so people haven't really shown that you need this complexity to actually sort of really scale up. But if you go really if you can really demonstrate at scale like across examples and samples that you have this sort of scaling behavior, then I think you have this buying into these models. And for these, of course, there's not so much at least inductive biases used. And so I do think we're going to hit this regime actually quite soon, and we do see this also in a few papers.
turns.zh: 是的，可以公平地说，早期我们有一些非常小、更有限的预测模型，先学习潜在空间，然后再加上扰动。然后，当这些真正大规模的基础模型表示出现时，每个人都相信了炒作，可能有点过度相信，然后，显然之后来了所谓的清醒期之类的。然后有一大堆论文出来，基本上说，嘿，也许甚至更线性的模型也做得很好。实际上现在我看到 gen 论文，早期我们已经有一些基准测试表明，这不是那么超级简单容易的任务，只是改进它。我认为有一点道理，在当前数据状态下，对于某些事情，比如你想预测细胞中 CRISPR 的效果，你可能不需要最花哨的模型。而如果你问一点，或者你想预测细胞类型之类的，你知道，对于那个，逻辑回归通常就够了。但如果你想预测更难的东西，例如在我们的 niche former 论文中，这是一个空间组学的基础模型，我们展示了一个我们引入的新任务，你说你有基因表达，你有单个细胞在潜在空间中的状态，你能预测其邻近细胞的基因表达状态吗？因为你知道，它们总是在交流，或者反过来。所以，它们总是在交流，因为你知道，它们互相交谈，你会在一个细胞中看到另一个细胞状态的残留。然后实际上这更难做，如果你有这些更难的任务，你需要更强的、更线性的东西，你尤其需要寻找更微妙的数据。所以，你的问题，你能发现更多信息吗？哪些类型的东西，我认为很大程度上取决于你最终问什么。当然，在自监督学习阶段，我认为我们绝对还没有找到最好的表示和学习方式。有很多复制 NLP 类型 LLM 中发生的事情，对吧？掩码自编码器总是典型的方法，但损失的类型、表示的类型，我认为人们还在争论。也许因为你知道，这通常是表格数据，所以你可以直接尝试表格基础模型和各种东西。现在有很多 JEPA 类型的方法，因为就像我们有一件事用对比学习。所以人们只是在玩弄损失，但也玩弄表示。我认为现在审稿人，至少我长期以来一直倡导这一点，真的更仔细地看，你真的正确展示了缩放定律。这是早期基础模型论文中缺失的，所以人们还没有真正展示你需要这种复杂性才能真正扩展。但如果你真的能在规模上展示，比如跨例子和样本，你有这种缩放行为，那么我认为人们就会相信这些模型。对于这些，当然，至少使用的归纳偏置不多。所以我确实认为我们实际上会很快达到这个状态，我们也在几篇论文中看到了这一点。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean you know, the ultimate thing of course you want to do is you want to be doing this perturbation prediction better cuz that's sort of what people now at least understand by virtual cell, right? And for this, I would not claim that pure representation learning is the right way to go. Sorry for making the subtlety again, but I think typically you learn the state space with these foundation models, but then sort of the way how they behave under an action under perturbation, this is where you need this more world model like type of approaches. turns.zh: 让我先把文化部分放一放，因为我觉得这是一个很难回答但非常好的问题。那么，我先谈谈我认为你问到的非常酷的一点，即这些事情的发生与深度整合有关。我认为我们目前面临的最激动人心的前沿之一，也许是一个机会，就是我们现在真的可以开始指导实验了。所以，以前我们构建这些人类细胞图谱时，我们有这种映射的方面。然后我们谈到了世界模型预测问题，对吧？所以，从映射我们走向了预测。但现在我们可以真正地去引导下一个实验，对吧？这一直是科学方法，你知道，把我们的假设放入循环中，然后对它做些什么，但坦率地说，很多时候论文以某个模型结束，对吧？也许是一些概念图，也许有一点验证。但然后你开始下一个项目，对吧？当然你学到了一点，但没有像持续学习那样的东西。但现在，我认为我们可以真正地越来越多地循环回来。这在分子设计或材料设计等领域非常常见。你有点像是在实验室在循环中被解决。尽管一些大型制药公司已经把这作为一个普遍的大主题，但没有很多例子真正人们做多个循环的这种实验、计算模型、然后回去的整合，无论这是现在两个人一个，对吧？但这种整合很难建立。而且很难建立一次，因为建模，因为实际上一旦你有了一个模型，决定什么是最优的下一个问题并不简单。我们实际上推出了一我认为今天或明天应该在 bioRxiv 上，我们称之为 Lab Compass 的新东西，它是一个逆向生成模型，实际上允许你一旦你有一个前向世界模型或其他什么，告诉你需要做什么才能达到某个状态。所以，这对我们来说非常令人兴奋，对吧？我认为工作的很大一部分不仅仅是模型，而是与实验人员的工作，在这个案例中是一位来自剑桥大学的好朋友和同事，他做造血作用。此外，有一个快速循环系统，我们实际上设置了三个四个实验室在循环中，我们迭代地改进模型。我认为这是一件非常困难的事情。这涉及到你的第二个问题，Brandon，对吧？比如你如何带来一种文化，一旦你的计算人员或模型或其他什么预测了某件事，你实际上要说服实验人员投入他们的时间，因为这些实验通常需要一些时间，对吧？真正接受并实际测量一些后续工作。有时你知道如果涉及分子，这效果会好一些，因为那样你知道风险也不那么高，但你知道如果你说现在你需要做这个新细胞，你需要添加这些非常奇怪的东西。你真的想这样做吗？我们是不是不应该凭直觉，然后你知道这些去中介化的解决方案就来了。所以我认为真正建立这个远非易事。这需要文化，可能是同一个人在做。很多人然后开始抛出机器人技术等等，但我认为这有点太早了，因为我们的实验的周期时间仍然有点长，但我确实认为这会到来，你知道显然最终的愿景是我们想要对一切进行强化学习。我们也想在这个循环中进行强化学习。这有点遥远，但你知道我认为我们正在慢慢接近。目前它更多可能是主动学习。
